title: Phone Stand
description: Illustrative example: geometry, pointer and words are authored, not recorded.

cues.label: I choose a wide base first so I can evaluate stability before fixing the viewing angle.
The depth matters more than the width: tapping the screen pushes the phone backwards.
The back panel is angled for viewing, but I keep the angle as one parameter so I can change its inclination if the phone or the context changes.
I add a shallow lip to prevent slipping while leaving room to reach the bottom of the device.
Higher than about a centimeter starts covering the screen.
Before moving to details, I soften the sharp base corners for handling while keeping enough flat contact for stability.
A large radius would eat into the footprint I chose in step 1.
The retaining lip should not block charging.
I cut a centered cable passage but keep support on both sides, so the phone still cannot slide.
I add a pair of narrow ribs near the sides instead of filling the entire area with material, and mirror one rib so both sides stay identical when I edit it.
Instead of making the base heavier, I use four small contact pads to increase friction and stabilize the stand on an uneven table.
Patterning one pad means I edit all four at once.
A solid back panel uses more material than needed.
I explore a central opening while retaining side rails, accepting that it may reduce stiffness — the ribs from step 6 make that acceptable.
I bring in a simplified phone proxy to check the viewing angle, charging access, and whether the lip clears the device before committing to dimensions.
The proxy is temporary and not printed.
